metadata.title: Price ceiling: binding cap, fixed curves, shortage
metadata.subject: Economics
metadata.objective: Show a binding price ceiling creating shortage without shifting supply or demand.
metadata.expectedUnderstanding: A maximum price below the equilibrium is binding: at that price the quantity supplied falls along the unchanged supply curve and the quantity demanded rises along the unchanged demand curve, so quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied and the shortage is Qd minus Qs measured at the cap. A cap at or above the equilibrium is not binding and changes nothing.

primitives.text: Price ceiling: a cap below equilibrium creates a shortage

checkpoints.prompt: The cap is at 8, below the equilibrium price. Did the demand curve move when the cap was imposed?
Continue to lower the cap and watch where the two quantities go.
At the capped price, which is larger: quantity demanded or quantity supplied?
If the cap were 11, above the equilibrium, what shortage would it create?

narration.text: Demand slopes down, supply slopes up; they cross at the equilibrium price, where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
A price ceiling is a legal maximum. At 8 it sits below the equilibrium, so it binds.
At the cap of 8, suppliers offer 16 and buyers want 28: the horizontal gap is a shortage of 12.
Now let the cap fall. Both quantities slide along the same two curves.
At a cap of 6, supply is 12 and demand is 36, so the shortage widens to 24.
The curves have not moved at all: only the cap moved, and the gap is measured at the capped price.
A cap at or above the equilibrium, the dashed line, is not binding: no shortage and no surplus.

fallback.text: Static supply-and-demand figure with linear curves Qd = 60 - 4P and Qs = 2P, equilibrium at P* = 10 and Q* = 20. Draw the cap at P = 8: at that price Qs = 16 and Qd = 28, so the shortage is 28 - 16 = 12, marked as a horizontal gap between the supply and demand curves. Repeat as a small table for caps 9, 8, 6, 5 giving shortages 6, 12, 24, 30, with the note that Qd and Qs are read off the same unchanged curves. A cap at 12 lies above P*, is not binding, and creates neither shortage nor surplus.

accessibility.alt: A price-quantity diagram with a downward demand line and an upward supply line crossing at the equilibrium dot E. A red dashed horizontal line is the price ceiling, below the equilibrium; at that height a red arrow runs from the supply curve to the demand curve and is labelled shortage. As the ceiling slides down, the arrow lengthens while both curves stay exactly where they were. A grey dashed line above the equilibrium shows a cap that does not bind.
accessibility.reducedMotion: Show two static panels of the same diagram: left with the cap at 8 and the shortage arrow labelled 12, right with the cap at 6 and the shortage labelled 24, with the S and D curves identically placed in both so the non-shift is visible.
